title: Retrieval Buy-In
author: Peps McCrea
summary: Peps McCrea, co-authoring with memory psychologist William Wadsworth, opens a new Snacks series on revision by tackling 'retrieval resistance' -- the fact that students often don't embrace retrieval practice even after being taught why it works. Retrieval strengthens memory far more than re-reading, but re-reading feels superior because it's effortless and mistake-free. Citing Wadsworth & Hibble (2023), McCrea notes 45% of students still default to re-reading or note-taking. His prescription: convince students retrieval actually works for them, normalize mistakes as a sign of productive effort, and flag the risk of unconscious procrastination -- elaborate flashcard-making or mind-mapping that feels like retrieval prep but isn't the practice itself.
points: McCrea's core distinction: retrieval means 'pulling information out' of memory (flashcards, free recall) versus 'putting it in' (re-reading), and pulling out strengthens memory and understanding far more.
Re-reading persists because it feels superior -- it requires less effort and produces no visible mistakes -- even though that absence of effort is exactly what makes it less effective.
Citing Wadsworth & Hibble (2023), he notes 45% of students still rely predominantly on re-reading or note-taking despite understanding that retrieval practice is more effective.

His three-part fix for 'retrieval resistance': convince students it works for them, normalise mistakes as expected and correctable, and flag unconscious procrastination as a disguised way of avoiding the harder retrieval work.
quotes: Retrieval practice has the potential to be powerful when it comes to revision. However, despite our efforts to educate students on this approach, it isn't always embraced wholeheartedly.

Most humans tend to assume that re-reading is more effective than retrieval. This kinda makes sense... re-reading requires less effort, and we can't really make any mistakes... as a result, it just feels superior.
A recent study by Wadsworth & Hibble (2023) found that 45% of students still rely predominantly on re-reading or note-taking.
Messaging that making mistakes is to be expected. And even a good indicator that you're pushing yourself.

Flagging the risk of unconscious procrastination. When faced with challenging tasks, we can easily find ourselves adopting sophisticated avoidance strategies, such as spending way too much time making the flash cards in the first place or creating beautifully illustrated mind maps!
